UKMTO’s November 24 warnings included a bulk carrier hit at anchor on November 22 and three tanker strikes late on November 22 UTC, which fall on November 23 Gulf time. JMIC also reported that U.S.-assisted transits rose from 27 to 38 per day, increasing exposure, though traffic remained well below its 2025 baseline. ([ukmto.org](https://www.ukmto.org/-/media/ukmto/products/20261120-ukmto_vra_overview_u.pdf))

**Why I don’t extrapolate the surge.** The strikes came in clusters, and I found no newer qualifying incident beyond November 23 Gulf time in the dated reporting available on November 25. That pulls the estimate **down** from the recent surge rate, although the latest warnings show why a reporting gap is not proof of a quiet day. The main risk to YES is that the next qualifying incident falls outside Friday’s 24-hour window, not that UKMTO publishes the report after Friday. ### 3. Strongest Reason the Obvious Outcome Might Fail
Even though the Strait of Hormuz is experiencing its heaviest week of attacks since the war began, the probability for a single 24-hour window (Friday, Nov 27, 00:00–23:59 GST) remains close to a coin toss. Because qualifying incidents tend to cluster against specific non-compliant convoys (e.g., three Sinokor VLCCs hit at 20:25 UTC on Nov 22/23, and two tankers hit on Nov 21), there are still multi-day gaps between UKMTO/JMIC-verified strikes. Consequently, either an operational pause on Friday or a refusal by struck vessels to submit verification to UKMTO/JMIC could easily result in zero qualifying reports for that specific date.

Balancing the intense late-November escalation (~70% of recent days seeing an attack) against clustering effects and UKMTO's verification bottleneck, I estimate a 55% chance of at least one qualifying incident occurring on November 27, 2026.
